summaries.example: Imagine two children who look and think alike. One lives where a real kind of liquid called water exists. The other lives where a look-alike liquid exists instead. Externalism says their word “water,” and perhaps their thoughts about it, could mean different things because their surroundings differ. This creates a puzzle: can each child know what they are thinking just by looking inward, without learning about the world outside?
summaries.summary: This entry explores a disagreement about the connection between the mind and the world. Externalism says that what a thought means can depend partly on things outside the thinker, such as water, other people, or a language community. Self-knowledge is our knowledge of our own thoughts. At first, these ideas seem to clash. If the meaning of a thought depends on the world, perhaps a person must investigate the world before knowing what the thought means. The entry examines arguments for this worry and several replies. One reply says that the needed facts about the environment may be learned through experience, not automatically from the meaning of a thought. Another says that some concepts can be empty, so a concept need not require a real object. A further reply says that an argument can have true starting points without giving us new knowledge in its conclusion. The entry also discusses a story in which a person is secretly moved from Earth to a similar planet. His word “water” slowly changes what it refers to, raising questions about memory and self-knowledge. Other philosophers answer that such a case is unusual, that some judgments about current thoughts verify themselves, or that self-knowledge does not work like observing an outside object. The debate does not have one agreed solution, but it helps philosophers study how minds, language, knowledge, and the world are connected.
key_ideas: Externalism says that the environment can help give thoughts their meaning.
A person may seem able to know their own thoughts simply by thinking about them.
The puzzle asks whether knowing the meaning of a thought also requires knowing facts about the outside world.
Some philosophers think externalism and armchair self-knowledge conflict; others think they can fit together.
Replies include saying that unusual cases are not relevant, that some self-judgments make themselves true, or that self-knowledge can sometimes depend on experience.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters because it asks how we can understand our own minds. It also connects everyday ideas about words and memory with deep questions about knowledge. Thinking carefully about the puzzle can show why philosophers use imaginary cases and why a disagreement may involve several different questions rather than one simple yes-or-no answer.

important_terms.definition: The idea that the world around us helps determine what our thoughts and words mean.
Knowing something about your own thoughts or feelings.
Knowledge gained without checking the outside world through observation or investigation.
A made-up case used to test an idea by imagining unusual circumstances.

questions_to_think_about: Could two people who are identical inside still mean different things because they live in different places?
Do you always need to check the world to know what you are thinking?
Would a strange thought experiment show something about everyday life?
Can saying “I am thinking this thought right now” help make the statement true?

summaries.example: Consider Oscar and his exact physical duplicate on Twin Earth. On Earth, the liquid called water is H2O; on Twin Earth, a different substance, XYZ, looks and behaves similarly. Although Oscar and Twin Oscar are internally alike, an externalist argues that “water” refers to different substances for them, so their water-thoughts have different contents. The pressure on self-knowledge appears when Oscar asks, without investigating his surroundings, whether his current thought concerns water rather than XYZ.
summaries.summary: The entry examines whether semantic externalism creates a problem for self-knowledge. Externalism about mental content says that the content of a thought is partly fixed by the thinker’s environment. Twin Earth cases are used to motivate this view: an Earth speaker and a physically similar counterpart may use the same word for different substances because their surroundings differ. If content depends on such external facts, it may seem that a thinker cannot know the content of a thought merely from the armchair. The main incompatibilist argument is a reductio. It combines externalism with armchair self-knowledge and argues that the result would be a priori knowledge of an environmental condition, even though that condition should be known empirically. Compatibilists challenge different parts of this reasoning. They question whether externalism entails the needed environmental claim a priori, defend externalism about concepts whose referents do not exist, or argue that warrant does not transmit through a deduction when the conclusion is already presupposed. Another response accepts that self-knowledge may have an empirical basis, while preserving some first-person advantage. A further possibility treats the unexpected armchair knowledge as a route to an anti-skeptical conclusion, though the entry notes difficulties for that interpretation. The second major challenge uses slow switching. Oscar is moved from Earth to Twin Earth, and his use of “water” gradually comes to concern XYZ. If he cannot detect the change from the armchair, perhaps he cannot know his own thought content. key_ideas: Twin Earth-style cases motivate externalism by imagining internally identical people whose environments differ, producing different reference and thought content.
The central tension is between EXT, the claim that environment partly determines content, and SK, the claim that a thinker can know content from the armchair.
The reductio argument claims that EXT plus SK would yield armchair knowledge of an empirical environmental condition, such as the existence of water.

Compatibilist replies question whether externalism supplies the relevant implication a priori, whether concepts can be empty, whether warrant transmits through the argument, or whether self-knowledge is partly empirical.
Slow-switching arguments claim that a person may be unable to discriminate between an original content and a twin content after an unnoticed environmental change.

Replies appeal to self-verifying judgments, relevant alternatives, theories of memory, the possibility that skeptical arguments undermine themselves, and anti-recognitional accounts of self-knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate links philosophy of mind, philosophy of language, and epistemology. It asks whether meanings are located entirely inside individual thinkers or partly in social and physical surroundings. It also tests what knowledge requires: truth, evidence, discrimination between alternatives, memory, or a special first-person standpoint. Even when the arguments do not settle the dispute, they clarify why claims about the mind can depend on theories of language and the world.

important_terms.definition: The view that the content or meaning of a mental representation is partly determined by relations to the external environment.
Knowledge a person has of their own mental states, such as what they are thinking or believing.
In this debate, knowledge gained without a concerted empirical investigation of the external world; introspective knowledge may still count as armchair knowledge.
A position holding that externalism and armchair self-knowledge cannot both be true.
A position holding that externalism and armchair self-knowledge can coexist.
A thought experiment in which a person is moved between Earth and a similar environment, causing a gradual change in what a term or thought refers to.
A judgment about a current thought that is true partly because making the judgment involves having that very thought.
The idea that an argument may fail to give new support to its conclusion even when the premises entail it, because accepting the premises already depends on the conclusion.

questions_to_think_about: Does a difference in reference necessarily show a difference in thought content?
If an argument’s conclusion is already presupposed when its premises are accepted, has the argument established anything new?
Should an unusual possibility such as slow switching count against ordinary knowledge?
Can memory preserve an earlier thought content when the surrounding environment changes?
Is self-knowledge more like observing an object, or more like expressing a commitment in thought and speech?

summaries.example: Suppose Maya and her identical twin live in two communities. In Maya’s community, the word “soda” means fizzy drinks made with sugar. In her twin’s community, the same word also includes a similar drink made with a different ingredient. The twins have had the same experiences inside their heads, but their surroundings and communities give the word different meanings. If Maya says, “I am thinking about soda,” can she know exactly what her thought means without checking which community and drink she is connected to?
summaries.summary: This entry studies whether externalism about thought content fits with self-knowledge. Externalism says that what a thought means depends partly on the thinker’s surroundings. The surroundings may include objects, other people, and the practices of a language community. Twin Earth examples make the idea vivid: two people can be alike in their inner states while using a word for different substances because they live in different environments. The challenge is that people often seem able to know what they are thinking simply by reflecting, without checking the outside world. The entry calls this armchair self-knowledge. One incompatibilist argument uses a reductio. If externalism says a water-thought requires a certain environmental condition, and if a thinker knows a priori that she is having that thought, she might seem able to know a priori that the environmental condition holds. But the condition appears empirical, so the two views seem to clash. Compatibilists answer in several ways. They question whether externalism really entails the needed condition a priori, discuss how a concept could refer to nothing, and argue that a valid-looking deduction may not provide new warrant when its conclusion is already assumed in the background. Some philosophers instead accept that self-knowledge can be empirical, while others suggest that externalism and self-knowledge might even help answer skeptical worries. A second challenge uses slow switching. A person is secretly moved from Earth to a similar planet, and the meaning of “water” gradually changes. Since the person may not notice, the case seems to show that she cannot identify her own thought content from the armchair. key_ideas: Externalists use cases like Twin Earth to argue that the same inner condition can have different meanings in different environments.
The main conflict is between externalism and the idea that people can know their own thought contents without investigating the world.
The reductio argument says that combining these views seems to produce a strange result: armchair knowledge of an outside-world fact.
Compatibilists respond that externalism may not give the needed a priori implication, or that the reasoning may fail to pass support from its premises to its conclusion.
Slow-switching cases focus on whether someone can tell which meaning their thoughts have after moving to a different environment.
Some philosophers defend self-knowledge by treating certain current self-judgments as self-verifying or by saying that bizarre alternatives are not normally relevant.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate matters because it connects the mind to language, society, and the physical world. It also shows that “knowing your own mind” may involve several abilities: knowing that you are thinking, knowing what content the thought has, and distinguishing that content from a close alternative. Philosophers use the debate to examine knowledge, memory, skepticism, and the limits of introspection.

important_terms.definition: The view that the outside world, including physical objects and language communities, helps determine what thoughts mean.
Knowledge about your own thoughts, beliefs, or other mental states.
Knowing something without carrying out an investigation of the outside world; in this debate, thinking about one’s own mind can count as this.
A disagreement about whether two claims can both be true.
A reasoning strategy that assumes claims are true and then tries to derive an obviously unacceptable result.
A case where a person is secretly moved between similar environments, so a word or thought slowly comes to refer to something different.
A judgment about a present thought that helps make itself true because the judgment involves having that thought.

questions_to_think_about: Can two people think different thoughts even when their brains and behavior are alike?
Does knowing what you are thinking require knowing what your words refer to?
When does an unusual possibility become relevant to what someone knows?
Could memory keep an old meaning, or would it change along with the new environment?
Are some kinds of self-knowledge automatic rather than discoveries made by inner observation?
